newsitem.title: GERMANY: German supreme court upholds Wall death sentences.
newsitem.headline: German supreme court upholds Wall death sentences.

text.p: Germany's supreme court ruled on Tuesday that former East German officials could be jailed in connection with the Cold War killings along the Berlin Wall and the former inner-German border.

The Federal Constitutional Court upheld a 1993 lower court verdict of murder against three former members of East Germany's National Defence Council who were responsible for the heavy fortifications and shoot-to-kill orders along the border.

It said former defence minister Heinz Kessler, his deputy Fritz Streletz and Suhl regional party boss Hans Albrecht must now start the jail sentences of five to 7-1/2 years the Berlin court imposed. They have been free during their appeal.
The long-awaited ruling meant the court did not agree with charges by former communist officials that united Germany practised "victors' justice" against them.

"With this decision, the supreme court justices have just about closed a chapter in the legal proceedings concerning East Germany's past," ARD television commented right after the court's ruling was made public. "There will probably be no room any more for any thoughts of amnesty.
"The justices have also contradicted the misconception that the courts nab the little fish but let the big ones swim away."

In a related case, the court also upheld a guilty verdict against a former border guard who killed a defector in a hail of machine gun bullets, saying such heavy fire could not be justified even by a young recruit acting on orders.

The extreme secrecy surrounding East Germany's fortified borders has made it impossible to know how many people were shot dead or killed by landmines as they tried to flee west from the 1950s to the fall of the Wall on November 9, 1989.
Berlin courts have convicted 29 lower-ranking border guards of murder but given most of them suspended sentences because they were young recruits following orders.
After German unification in 1990, Berlin courts have tried but failed to convict high-level officials for the killings.
Former communist leader Erich Honecker was let off on health grounds and the trial of several other Politburo members is hampered by the lack of proof they ordered guards to shoot.

Six former East German army generals in charge of border security were sentenced in September to prison terms between three to six years for instructing guards on how to shoot and lay mines to stop refugees.

In another trial in Berlin, East Germany's last communist leader, Egon Krenz, and three other Politburo members are charged with murder on the grounds that they did not use their power to ease the tough military restrictions along the border.
Krenz has argued in his defence that the Soviet Union controlled all matters dealing with the border, the westernmost frontier of the Warsaw Pact, and East German leaders had no say in the issue.
